Infrastructure, Equipment, IT, HR, Policies & procedures, and Financial resources checks have been conducted in thousands of facilities across 77 countries, scoring each against hundreds of supply chain checks.

. . .

[Which of those checks actually go with vaccines being in good condition? That is what I set out to answer.]{.remember}

::: {.notes}
About 60 seconds. Start with the picture and talk through it: the fridge on the left is what an assessor sees; on the right are three opened vials from that fridge. One was dated when it was opened and is still inside its window. One has no date at all, so nobody in that clinic can say whether it is safe. One is past the window and should already have been thrown away. Then the scale line, then read the question and pause.
:::

## One assessment, three components, and this is about Quality

The WHO Effective Vaccine Management assessment scores a facility against hundreds of checks, each with a code like `R0290` called requirements. It also scores a set of outcomes.

- Outcomes are **availability**, **efficiency**, and **quality**. This analysis is about **quality**.
- The applied goal is a shorter instrument, an **EVM-Lite**. If a short checklist could check only a few things, which ones should they be?

::: {.notes}
About 45 seconds. Define requirement once, out loud, because every later slide uses the word. Then the division of labour in one breath. Land on EVM-Lite as the destination: that is what the whole talk is walking towards.
:::

The composite score `QU` is the combination of them all.

::: {.notes}
About 70 seconds, and it earns the time because everything later refers back to this grid. Take the timeline first: a vial is opened at the left mark, doses can be given for 28 days, and anything left after the right mark is waste. Then read the grid as a table. Down the left are the three ways a vaccine goes bad: it expires, it gets too hot, which the vial monitor shows by darkening past its discard point, or it sits opened for too long. Across the top is where the assessor catches it, either watching a real immunisation session or inspecting what is in the fridge. Each failure is checked both ways, which gives six requirements, and the composite QU pools all six. Say that the two in blue are the ones I follow, and that the reason the other four fade out is coming in a couple of slides. Worth flagging now that the left column can only be scored when a session is running, because that fact comes back later to explain a strange result.
:::

## The aim here is to explain, not to predict or forecast 

Following Shmueli (2010), the question here is which requirements go with quality and explain the variations in qualituy, not how to predict a facility's score. [^1]

- Error metrics such as RMSE will not be reported because a small error would not tell me which requirement matters
- Only models that hand back a **readable number per requirement** are allowed to give the answer

[^1]: Shmueli, G. (2010). To explain or to predict? *Statistical Science*, 25(3), 289-310.

::: {.notes}
About 40 seconds. Say why the distinction bites: a model can be excellent at guessing scores and still tell you nothing you could act on. That rule disqualifies a model later that fits better than the one I use, and I want the panel to see the rule before they see the casualty.
:::

## How to read every number I show

- **R squared on unseen facilities.** Facilities differ in quality. R squared is the share of that difference a fitted model accounts for, from 0 for none to 1 for all. It is always measured on facilities the model was never fitted on.
- **Effect.** The change in the quality score, which runs from 0 to 1, for one standard deviation more of a requirement's score. The causal section later uses a plainer unit: the change from not met to met in full.
- **Conclusive.** The model is refitted on 200 random resamples of the facilities. A requirement is conclusive when the middle 95% of its effects across those refits lies on one side of zero, and at least half of the refits keep it in the model at all.
- **Not applicable.** Where a requirement does not apply to a facility, the linear models are given the column's mean. The checks later remove those filled cells and look again.

::: {.notes}
About 60 seconds. This slide buys back time everywhere else, so do not rush it. The resamples idea in plain speech: shuffle which facilities you happen to look at, refit, and see whether the answer keeps pointing the same way. Say that the mean filling is new in this version of the analysis, and that a later slide removes it to check.
:::

## The year column is really a country label

Every one of the 77 countries was assessed in exactly one year. Not one country appears in two different years.

- So the year tells which group of countries a facility belongs to, and nothing about change over time
- If the year looks important later, it means countries assessed in some years score better than countries assessed in others

::: {.notes}
- I keep the column, but I never read it as a trend, and this comes back twice
::: 

::: {.notes}
About 35 seconds. Small check, large consequence. Flag now that the year turns out to matter for both components, so when it appears the panel already knows how to read it. Without this slide that result looks like a story about improvement over time, which would be wrong.
:::

## Four of the seven targets have almost nothing to explain {.tbl}

```{=html}
<table class="dt l" data-quarto-disable-processing="true"><colgroup><col style="width:56%"><col style="width:22%"><col style="width:22%"></colgroup><thead><tr><th>Target</th><th class="r">Facilities at full marks</th><th class="r">Best R² on unseen facilities</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>R0712</code> vials used within 28 days of opening</td><td class="r">54.9%</td><td class="r">0.187</td></tr><tr><td><code>R0722</code> no opened vials kept beyond 28 days</td><td class="r">54.5%</td><td class="r">0.171</td></tr><tr><td><code>QU</code> composite quality score</td><td class="r">58.2%</td><td class="r">0.059</td></tr><tr><td><code>R0710</code> <code>R0711</code> <code>R0713</code> <code>R0716</code> expired or heat-damaged vaccine</td><td class="r">94 to 97%</td><td class="r">0.05 or below</td></tr></tbody></table>
```

**The composite and the two vial components are carried forward.** Almost every facility already passes the four expired and heat-damaged checks, so there is no variation left to explain.

::: {.notes}
About 60 seconds. Read the table row by row. The near-universal pass on expired and heat-damaged stock is a finding in itself about the last mile. What still separates facilities is multi-dose vial handling. The R squared figures here come from five repeated splits of the facilities; the next slide uses twenty.
:::

## The best-fitting model is not useful

Eleven model families, each run over twenty repeated splits of the facilities into 75% for fitting and 25% for testing.

- Random forest has the best raw test score, 0.239 on `R0712`, but it scores about 0.65 higher on the facilities it was fitted on. It memorises them.
- XGBoost fits its training facilities perfectly, 1.000, and does worse on new ones. Tree models cannot answer an explanatory question here.
- Among the models that give a readable number per requirement, **the elastic net wins all three targets**: [0.051]{.strong-blue} for `QU`, [0.191]{.strong-blue} for `R0712`, [0.180]{.strong-blue} for `R0722`.

::: {.notes}
About 65 seconds. This is the rule from the earlier slide biting. Random forest wins on paper and still loses, and I want that said plainly. The elastic net is worth one sentence: it keeps a small number of requirements and pushes the rest to exactly zero, so what comes out is already a short list.
:::

Between a fifth and two fifths of all variation sits between countries: 21% for the composite, 41% and 41% for the components. That is income and infrastructure, and no facility can act on it. Once country is in the model every requirement number becomes a within-country comparison, which hides how small the requirement signal really is. So I pay the price of the pale bars on purpose.

## How the ten least useful requirements were chosen

The bottom of a list is harder to define than the top, because the elastic net sets many effects to exactly zero and nothing orders them. So the rule has three steps, applied to each target separately.

1. **Set aside requirements with no room to vary**: those met in full by fewer than 5% or more than 95% of the facilities where they apply.
2. **Among the rest, take the ten kept in the fewest of the 200 resamples.** A requirement the model drops almost every time is one it has no use for.
3. **Break ties by the smallest average effect, then by the weakest raw correlation with the target.**

::: {.notes}
About 45 seconds. The WHO team asked for this as a credibility check: a method that ranks sensibly at the top should rank sensibly at the bottom too. Explain why step 1 is needed: a requirement everyone meets would otherwise land at the bottom for the wrong reason. The correlation is only a tie-breaker; it is not what the model uses.
:::

## Shuffling the answers finds almost nothing, so the real counts mean something

- The target scores were shuffled at random across facilities and the whole method was run again, ten times per target.
- Real counts: **2, 4 and 5** conclusive requirements. On shuffled scores: one false alarm in thirty runs, on the composite, and none on the components.
- The largest effect any shuffled run produced is a noise ceiling: 0.0063, 0.0238 and 0.0192. Every conclusive effect clears its ceiling.

::: {.notes}
About 60 seconds. If the method found requirements out of pure noise, then finding them in the real data would prove nothing. It found one in thirty tries. The noise ceiling is a second, gentler bar: anything below it could have come from noise. Everything conclusive is above it, and on R0722 so is one more, training to monitor supply chain performance.
:::

## Removing the filled-in values changes little

Where a requirement does not apply, the model was given the column's mean. Refitting only on facilities where the leading requirements were actually scored:

- All 11 leading effects keep their direction, and 8 stay conclusive.
- The three that lose the flag are the discard time on the composite, and training and fire extinguishers on `R0712`. Their effects shrink but keep their sign.
- The check keeps 1,810 of 2,258 facilities on the composite, 1,066 of 1,077 on `R0712` and 1,039 of 1,098 on `R0722`.

::: {.notes}
About 45 seconds. This defends the one compromise in the data preparation. Be straight that the discard-time requirement on the composite halves without its filled rows; it stays positive, and it comes back strongly in the causal section.
:::

Take `R0040`, having enough cold storage. **90%** of facilities meet it. Those that do are asked the multi-dose vial questions **11 points more often**, and they average **0.890** against **0.938** for those that do not.

::: {.notes}

Box two: those are the questions facilities actually fail, and you can only fail a question you were asked. Box three: a facility with spare fridge capacity is a facility running sessions. Box four: so the better equipped facility sits the harder test and can score lower for a reason that has nothing to do with its vaccines.

## Double machine learning {.tbl}

Take one requirement, say *staff know the discard time*, as the **treatment**. The quality score is the **outcome**. Every other column is a **control**.

1. **Predict the outcome from the controls** and keep what is left over, the residual.
2. **Predict the treatment from the controls** and keep its residual.
3. **Fit a straight line through the two residuals.** Its slope is the effect.

This association does not come from any control, hence causal effect.

**Unit:** the change in the score when a facility goes from not meeting the requirement to meeting it in full.

::: {.notes}
About 90 seconds. This is the one slide that has to land. Use the discard-time example all the way through. Steps 1 and 2 strip out everything the other 171 columns can explain; step 3 asks whether what is left still moves together. Both predictions are made by elastic nets, the same kind of model as before. Then the unit: not a coefficient per standard deviation any more, but the gap between a facility whose staff know the rule and an otherwise similar facility whose staff do not.
:::

## How a result counts, and how country is handled {.tbl}

- **q-value.** A p-value corrected for testing about 170 columns at once. **Conclusive means q below 0.05**.
- **Thin evidence.** A column asked of under a quarter of facilities, or answered the same way by over 95% of them, is shown but never flagged.


::: {.notes}
About 80 seconds. Three definitions and one decision. Leaving country out lets differences between countries, in policies, supply systems and assessment teams, show up as requirement effects. Centring every column within its country throws those away and asks only whether a facility that meets the requirement does better than its neighbours in the same country. That is the fairer test and the part a country programme can act on, which is why the verdict rests on it, and why effects shrink when it is applied.
:::

::: {.notes}
About 90 seconds. Read the three shaded rows first: knowing the discard time on both components, knowing the storage principles, knowing the types of opened-vial wastage. Each keeps about half its size within countries: half of the association came from differences between countries and half from facilities of the same country. Then the three that fail: cold storage passes every statistical check but has no route to a vial and is explained by exposure; salaries keep 30% within countries and are the effect a hidden factor could move most; the negative training effect collapses from 20 points to 7 as soon as the other training requirements leave the controls.
:::

```

On `R0712` the fractional logit edges the elastic net by less than the variation between splits. That counts as a tie, so **the elastic net is used for all three targets** and the two levels can be compared.

About 55 seconds. Fourteen averages carry less information than the 170 items they summarise, so the fit drops; the ordering of the targets does not change. The tree models still memorise. Country matters even more at this level, and the unseen-country figures are again the honest ones.

## The subcategory results pass the same stress tests

- **Shuffled scores.** Thirty shuffled runs produced no conclusive subcategory, and every conclusive effect clears its noise ceiling.
- **Filled-in values.** All ten conclusive effects keep their direction and their flag.

::: {.notes}
About 70 seconds. The same four checks as at requirement level. The noise ceilings are 0.0063, 0.0194 and 0.0160. The disagreement on the composite is worth saying out loud: with only fourteen columns the elastic net and the tree families spread their choices differently, and the composite is where every method has least to work with. Buildings are named by only two families on R0712. Almost no facility has a filled cell at this level, which is why the filled-value check changes nothing.
:::

```

[Effect: change in points out of 100 when the subcategory goes from its lowest possible score to its highest. A whole range is a large move, so a quarter of the knowledge range, 13 points on `R0712` and 17 on `R0722`, is the realistic figure to quote.]{.smallnote}

::: {.notes}
About 60 seconds. On R0722 the three conclusive subcategories are the screening's three. On R0712 only written procedures clears the line; knowledge has the largest effect, 51 points over its full range, but its q-value sits at 0.053, just outside. On the composite nothing is conclusive, and cold storage equipment is again the largest effect, downwards. One level up, the answer is the same: what staff know carries the two vial targets.
:::

## What the evidence supports

- Out of 170 requirements across 77 countries, quality at the last mile comes down to a handful, and **what staff know seems significant**: the discard time of multi-dose vials, the principles of vaccine storage, and the types of opened-vial wastage, as those three pass every test in the analysis.
- The composite score is a weak target. Its one conclusive effect, cold storage capacity, is a measurement artefact: better equipped facilities sit the harder test.

::: {.notes}
About 70 seconds. Four sentences, slowly. The first is the headline. The second is why it can be believed: conclusive after adjustment, about half the effect intact within countries, beyond the reach of any measured stand-in for a hidden factor, unmoved when their neighbours leave the controls, and each with a direct route to an opened vial. The third is what the causal section removed. The fourth is the honest reading of the composite.
:::

## What the evidence does not support, and what comes next

**The causal estimates hold only if nothing unmeasured drives both a requirement and quality.** 

**Article Suggestion:** 

- 1. Screening and causal effect analysis on the requirements dataset for R0712 and R0722.
- 2. The same analysis on the subcategories dataset.
- 3. Treat the other 4 quality components as anomaly detection problems and identify requirements and categories that lead to NOT HAVING a good quality component score.


::: {.notes}
About 45 seconds. End on the next step with the new assessments: a list fixed in advance and tested on countries that had no say in it is the one test that would settle the question. If asked about the controls: the follow-up chooses them for each requirement from the structure of the EVM framework, so that consequences of a requirement are never held fixed.
:::

# Thank you. Questions welcome. {.graylight}

## Backup: choosing the model

- Eleven families over the same twenty splits: ordinary least squares, ridge, LASSO, elastic net, fractional logit, a gamma model on the shortfall from full marks, boosted trees, bagged trees, randomised-split trees, XGBoost, and the mean of the training data as a floor.
- Plain least squares is the weakest linear model on unseen facilities for every target, so the penalties earn their place.
- The elastic net and the LASSO tie on every target; the elastic net is reported because it handles groups of near-identical requirements more gracefully.

::: {.notes}
For questions on model choice. One line on AIC if pushed: a criterion computed inside the sample rewards exactly the hard fitting that repeated splits exist to discount.
:::

## Backup: how the values that do not exist are handled

- Some requirements do not apply to a facility, and a linear model still needs a number in that cell.
- Two options were compared: fill with the column's mean, or fill and add a marker column saying the value was filled.
- The markers fit slightly better and double the number of columns, and a marker coefficient is not something a manager can act on, so the simple fill is kept.
- Two checks limit the cost: the tree families that need no filling name the same requirements, and refitting on fully scored facilities keeps every leading direction.

::: {.notes}
For questions on missing data. Be straight: markers win narrowly on fit and lose on usefulness.
:::

## Backup: quality as four ordered bands

- The composite score was cut at 0.6, 0.8 and 0.95, and 58% of facilities land in the top band.
- Always naming the biggest band beats the ordinal model on plain accuracy, 0.582 against 0.496, and the model's agreement with the truth beyond chance is 0.092, weak by any usual standard.
- The top twenty requirements change under banding while no measure of fit improves, so the analysis keeps the continuous score.

::: {.notes}
For questions about whether the continuous score is the right framing.
:::
